caption:
Why was Tesla's Wardenclyffe Tower never finished?

In March 1901 J. P. Morgan signed a contract giving Nikola Tesla $150,000 to build a wireless station on Long Island capable of sending messages to London and to ships at sea. Morgan took a 51% interest in the company and in the patents.

Tesla's system did not use radio waves. He doubted Hertzian waves existed, and if they did, he believed they would travel straight out into space and be "hopelessly lost." Instead he wanted to inject current into the ground at the right frequency and make the whole planet resonate. In his own words, the buried works were meant "to have a grip on the earth so the whole of this globe can quiver."

Then he read a June 1901 article by Marconi and decided to scale everything up: a more powerful transmitter, image and telephone transmission, wireless power. He asked Morgan for much more money. Morgan refused and demanded an accounting of what had been spent.

On July 3, 1903 Tesla wrote: "Will you help me or let my great work — almost complete — go to pots?" Morgan answered on July 14 that he would not make further advances. Newspapers reported that on the night of that reply, and several nights after, the tower shot off bright flashes that lit up the sky. Wardenclyffe never seemed to operate again. The project was abandoned in 1906 and never became operational.

The tower was dynamited for scrap on July 4, 1917 by the Smiley Steel Company. It took until September to bring it down. Scrap value: $1,750. A wartime rumor claimed the government ordered it destroyed because German spies were using it — Tesla could not correct it, because the mortgages and foreclosure had been kept off the public record to hide his finances.

Still unresolved: the meaning of those flashes was never explained by Tesla or his workers. There are descriptions of four 100-foot tunnels radiating from the base of a 120-foot shaft; speculation ranges from drainage to access to enhancing the ground connection, perhaps filled with salt water or liquid nitrogen. And how Tesla intended to combine his ground conduction and atmospheric methods at Wardenclyffe is unknown. Tesla kept the press and public away, so little is known.

cards.note: This photo was taken in 1904 so Tesla could go back to J. P. Morgan and ask for the money to finish the tower.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe Tower - 1904.jpg. Author unknown. Public domain.
cards.alt: Tall wooden lattice tower with a domed top standing above a low brick building.

cards.headline: He was not <y>sending radio waves</y>.
cards.note: Tesla doubted Hertzian waves existed, and thought that if they did they would travel straight into space and be "hopelessly lost." His plan was to drive current into the Earth and use the planet itself as the conductor.
cards.source: File:US patent 1119732-001.png, diagram by Nikola Tesla. Public domain.
cards.alt: Line-drawn patent diagram sheet showing apparatus for transmitting electrical energy.

cards.headline: <y>120 feet down</y>, sixteen iron pipes.
cards.note: Descriptions, some from Tesla's 1923 foreclosure testimony, record a wood and steel lined shaft sunk 120 feet beneath the tower. At the bottom, machines pushed iron pipes out 300 feet. The purpose, Tesla said, was "to have a grip on the earth so the whole of this globe can quiver."
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe Tower.jpg, circa 1902. Author not recorded. Public domain.
cards.alt: Base of the unfinished tower and brick laboratory building, with a rail car alongside.

cards.headline: Morgan said no. That night <y>the tower lit up</y>.
cards.note: Tesla wrote asking Morgan whether he would help or let "my great work — almost complete — go to pots." Morgan replied he was not disposed to make further advances. Newspapers reported that on that night, and several after, the tower shot off bright flashes lighting the sky. No explanation ever came.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe Tower - 1904.jpg. Author unknown. Public domain.
cards.alt: Close view of the domed cupola and upper timber framing of the Wardenclyffe tower.

cards.headline: Dynamited for scrap. Value: <y>one thousand seven hundred fifty dollars</y>.
cards.note: The Smiley Steel Company of New York began demolition on July 4, 1917. The first blast only knocked the tower onto a tilt; it was not fully down until September. A wartime rumor said the government ordered it destroyed because of German spies. The real reason was foreclosure.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe tower tesla new york demolition july september 1917.png, attributed to the American Press Association. Public domain.
cards.alt: The tower partly collapsed and leaning, its frame broken, after being dynamited.

cards.headline: Four tunnels. <y>Still no agreed explanation</y>.
cards.note: Tesla kept the press and public away from the site, so little is known about what was built underground. Descriptions mention four 100-foot tunnels radiating from the shaft. Guesses include drainage, access, or improving the ground connection, possibly filled with salt water or liquid nitrogen. How Tesla meant to combine his ground and atmospheric methods here is unknown.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe Tower.jpg, circa 1902. Author not recorded. Public domain.
cards.alt: Full view of the unfinished Wardenclyffe tower and its brick building in open ground.
